BBC, 26 November 12:35 GMT

Multimillion-pound A38 scheme shelved by government

The multi-million pound scheme would have created flyovers and underpasses at the Little Eaton, Markeaton and Kingsway roundabouts

A 3D rendering of the A38 upgrade project near Markeaton Park

The government has announced a major project to increase the capacity of the A38 in Derby will not go ahead.

The estimated £600m A38 scheme was approved by the government in July 2025, and would have seen roads widened, with flyovers and underpasses constructed at the Little Eaton, Markeaton and Kingsway roundabouts.

Earlier in the year, the government had said the scheme - along with a project to improve the A46 in Nottinghamshire - could be scrapped in order to pay for increased defence spending.

On Thursday the government confirmed it had decided to \"prioritise crucial investment to our national defence, now and for the future\".

The government said it had taken the decision \"having taken into account the consultation responses, input from National Highways and supporting evidence relating to a wide range of factors such as safety, housing, economic growth, value for money, environment and deliverability and investment considerations\".

Labour mayor of the East Midlands Claire Ward described the cancellation of the scheme, along with the shelving of the A46 Newark Bypass in Nottinghamshire, as \"short-sighted\".

Claire Ward was elected mayor of the East Midlands in 2024

\"We all have a part to play in keeping our country safe, but security is not strengthened by weakening, disproportionally, the infrastructure in the East Midlands that supports it,\" Ward said.

\"Losing investment into these schemes undermines this region to do what is being asked of us: grow the economy, create jobs, and stand on our own two feet. This is now much harder to achieve than we thought it would be at the start of the summer.

\"It is why cross-party regional politicians, businesses, and residents came together to make the case for these investments: they can see what the government cannot.

\"It is also why I offered to review the scope of the A38 and to cover the first phase of the A46 from East Midlands Combined County Authority (EMCCA) resources. Both felt like an appropriate offer given the demands of the Defence Investment Plan.

\"It is hard to see what more we could have done to help government do right by the East Midlands.\"

Ward said she would now discuss investing up to £100m of EMCCA resources to develop \"local solutions\" for both the A38 and A46 schemes.

Nadine Peatfield, leader of Derby City Council and deputy mayor of the EMCCA, said the cancellation was a \"disappointing decision\" for Derby.

\"Whatever views people held on the original A38 scheme, losing hundreds of millions of pounds of Government investment in our city is a significant setback,\" she said.

\"As a city with nationally important rail, manufacturing and defence industries, Derby relies on strong transport connections to support economic growth and opportunity.

\"We will continue to work with East Midlands Combined County Authority and other regional partners to identify and deliver a solution that our city deserves.\"

A Department for Transport spokesperson said it would continue working with Ward to \"support investment and infrastructure\" and \"take forward improvements to the A46 and A38 in the future\".

\"We have had to make difficult decisions on road spending to prioritise crucial investment to our national defence,\" said the spokesperson.

\"We continue to support growth in every postcode, which is why we are providing nearly £5bn in this year alone on our motorways and key A-roads to support maintenance, enhancement, and ensure smoother journeys.\"

Gail Roberts and her 14 neighbours were given compulsory purchase orders to make way for the A38 expansion

There are now questions as to what will happen to homes that were boarded up to make way for the scheme.

Gail Roberts was the last remaining resident of Queensway in Derby after her home was among 15 included in a compulsory purchase order for the project.

Many of her neighbours accepted it and moved out, leaving her \"stuck in a lovely house in a derelict street\".

Following an \"absolutely infuriating\" two-year dispute over the value of the house, she eventually accepted £40,000 less than an independent valuation she had been given.

Roberts said it had been \"painful\" to see her old home boarded up for the past three years, and for months she \"diverted halfway around Derby\" to avoid passing it.

The Stop the A38 Expansion Group had previously called for the properties to be restored and returned to use.

Former Mid Derbyshire Conservative MP Pauline Latham said she was \"worried\" about what would happen to the properties now.

She said: \"Are they all going to be knocked down under a new housing scheme, are they going to be brought back into use because they should be, but that'll cost money, and where's that going to come from?\"

Latham also told the BBC she was \"really angry\" with the cancellation and predicted traffic on the A38 will worsen.

\"It'll probably be 20 years before it comes back, but eventually the situation will be so congested it will have to,\" she said.

\"The queues to get out at rush hour now are impossible and it's only going to get worse.

\"We've got to have better roads, we've got to improve roads for motorists, and for other people, and this was going to improve for everybody.\"
